turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: That's super interesting. I'd love to talk to these people, both in the more bucket and the less bucket just to understand. Did you get to follow up with any of them?
turns.zh: 这太有意思了。我很想和这些人聊聊，无论是满意度高的人还是低的人。你们有没有跟他们做过后续调查？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A few people replied, and we're actually doing a followup poll that we'll look to in the show notes of going deeper into some of the stuff. But a lot ... There's the factors that make it more fun and less fun. The designers, they didn't share a lot actually of just the people that [inaudible 00:45:33]. I actually asked just like, "Why are you enjoying your job less?" I didn't hear a lot. So, I'm curious what's going on there.
turns.zh: 有几个人回复了。我们实际上正在做后续调查，相关内容会在节目笔记中深入探讨。不过很多人……有些因素让工作更有趣，也更无趣。比如设计师，他们分享得不多。实际上我问过他们："为什么你对工作满意度降低了？"没听到太多反馈。所以我很好奇这里面到底怎么回事。

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: Yeah. I'm seeing this a little bit with ... At Anthropic, I think everyone is fairly technical. This is something that we screen for when people join. There's a lot of technical interviews that people go through even for non-technical functions. (00:45:53): And our designers largely code. So, I think for them this is something that they have enjoyed from what I've seen, because now instead of bugging engineers they can just go in and code. And even some designers that didn't code before have just started to do it, and for them it's great, because they can unblock themselves. (00:46:12): But I'd be really interested just to hear more people's experiences, because I bet it's not uniform like that.
turns.zh: 是的。我在Anthropic也看到类似情况。我觉得这里每个人都相当技术型。这是我们招聘时筛选的条件。即使是非技术岗位，求职者也要经历大量技术面试。（00:45:53）：而且我们的设计师大多会编程。所以据我观察，他们很享受这个过程，因为现在他们不用去打扰工程师，自己就能直接编码了。甚至一些之前不编程的设计师也开始动手了，这对他们来说很棒，因为能解放自己的生产力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So, maybe if you're listening to this leave a comment if you're finding your job is less fun, and you're enjoying your job less, because what you're saying and what I'm hearing from most people, 70% of PMs and engineers are loving their job more. Like, if you're [inaudible 00:46:30] bucket, you could ... Something's going on.
turns.zh: 是啊。所以，也许如果你正在听这个节目，如果你发现自己的工作没那么有趣，工作满意度降低了，就留言分享一下吧。因为你所说的和我们从大多数人那里听到的情况一样，70%的产品经理和工程师都更热爱自己的工作。比如，如果你用[听不清00:46:30]工具，你可以……肯定有问题。

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. We do see that people use also different tools. So, for example, our designers they use the Claude desktop app a lot more to do their coding. So, you just download the desktop app. There's a code tab. It's right next to Cowork. (00:46:45): And it's actually the same as at Claude Code. So, it's the same agent, and everything. We've had this for many, many months. And so, you can use this to code in a way that you don't have to open a bunch of terminals. But you still get the power of Claude Code, and the biggest thing is you can just run as many Claude sessions in parallel as you want. We call this multi-Claude-ing. (00:47:04): So, it's a little more native I think for folks that are not engineers, and really this is back to bringing the product to where the people are. You don't want to make people use a different workflow. You don't want to make them go out of their way to learn a new thing. It's whatever people are doing, if you can make that a little bit easier, then that's just going to be a much better product that people enjoy more. (00:47:23): And this is just this principle of latent demand, which I think is just the single-most important principle in product.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。我们确实发现人们会使用不同的工具。比如，我们的设计师更多地使用Claude桌面应用来进行编码。只需下载桌面应用，点击代码标签，就在Cowork旁边（00:46:45）。实际上和Claude Code是一样的，使用相同的代理等。我们已经推出了这个功能好几个月了。这样你就不用打开一堆终端就能进行编码了，但还能享受Claude Code的强大功能，最重要的是你可以并行运行任意数量的Claude会话，我们称之为多Claude模式（00:47:04）。所以，我觉得对于非工程师用户来说，这更符合他们的使用习惯。关键在于让产品贴近用户的实际场景，不让用户改变工作流程，不让他们费力学习新东西。只要能让用户更轻松地完成现有任务，产品就会更受欢迎。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you talk about that actually? Because I was going to go there. Explain what this principle is and just what happens when you unlock this latent demand.
turns.zh: 你能具体讲讲这个原理吗？因为我正想问这个问题。解释一下这个原理是什么，以及当你激发这种潜在需求时会发生什么。

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: Latent demand is this idea that if you build a product in a way that can be hacked, or can be misused by people in a way it wasn't really designed for to do something that they want to do, then this helps you as the product builder learn where to take the product next. (00:47:55): So, an example of this is Facebook Marketplace. So, the manager for the team Fiona, she was actually the founding manager for the Marketplace team and she talks about this a lot. Facebook Marketplace is based on the observation back in ... This must have been, like, 2016 or something like this. That 40% of posts in Facebook groups are buying and selling stuff. (00:48:17): So, this is crazy. It's, like, people are abusing the Facebook groups product to buy and sell, and it's not abuse in a security sense. It's abuse in that no one designed the product for this, but they're figuring it out, because it's just so useful for this. (00:48:29): And so, it's pretty obvious. If you build a better product to let people buy and sell, they're going to like it. And it was just very obvious that Marketplace would be a hit from this. And so, the first thing was buy and sell groups, so, special purpose groups to let people do that, and the second product was Marketplace. (00:48:45): Facebook Dating I think started in a pretty similar place. And I think the observation was if you look at profile views, so, people looking at each other's profiles on Facebook, 60% of profile views were people that are not friends with each other that are opposite gender. And so, this traditional dating setup, people are just creeping on each other. So, maybe if you can build a product for this, it might work. (00:49:11): And so, this idea of latent demand I think is just so powerful. And, for example, this is also where Cowork came from. We saw that for the last six months or so, a lot of people using Claude Code were not using it to code. There was someone on Twitter that was using it to grow tomato plants. There was someone else using it to analyze their genome. Someone was using it to recover photos from a corrupted hard drive that was, like, wedding photos. There was someone that was using it for I think ... They were using it to analyze an MRI. (00:49:43): So, there's just all these different use cases that are not technical at all, and it was just really obvious. Like, people are jumping through hoops to use a terminal to do this thing. Maybe we should just build a product for them. (00:49:55): And we saw this actually pretty early. Back in maybe May of last year, I remember walking into the office and our data scientist Brendan had a Claude Code on his computer. He just had a terminal up. And I was shocked. I was like, "Brendan, what are you doing?" He figured out how to open the terminal, which is ... It's a very engineer-y product. Even a lot of engineers don't want to use a terminal. It's just the lowest level way to do your work. Just really, really in the weeds of the computer. (00:50:26): And so, he figured out how to use the terminal. He downloaded [inaudible 00:50:28]. He downloaded Claude Code. And he was doing SQL analysis in the terminal. It was crazy. And then the next week all of the data scientists were doing the same thing. (00:50:36): So, when you see people abusing the product in this way, using it in a way that it wasn't designed in order to do something that is useful for them, it's just such a strong indicator that you should just build a product and people are going to like that. It's something that's special purpose for that. (00:50:50): I think now there's also this interesting second dimension to latent demand. This is the traditional framing is look at what people are doing, make that a little bit easier, empower them. (00:50:59): The modern framing that I've been seeing in the last six months is a little bit different. And it's look at what the model is trying to do, and make that a little bit easier. (00:51:10): And so, when we first started building Claude Code, I think a lot of the way that people approached designing things with LLMs is they put the model in a box, and they were like, "Here's this application that I want to build. Here's the thing that I wanted to do, a model, you're going to do this one component of it. Here's the way that you're going to interact with these tools and APIs," and whatever. (00:51:28): And for Claude Code, we inverted that. We said, "The product is the model. We want to expose it. We want to put the minimal scaffolding around it. Give it the minimal set of tools. So, it can do the things, it can decide which tools to run. It can decide in what order to run them in," and so on. (00:51:41): And I think a lot of this was just based on latent demand of what the model wanted to do. And so, in research we call this being on distribution. You want to see what the model is trying to do. In product terms, latent demand is just the same exact concept but applied to a model.
turns.zh:
潜在需求指的是这样一种现象：如果你设计的产品可以被黑客攻击，或被用户以非预期的方式加以利用，以实现他们自己的需求，这实际上能帮助产品开发者发现产品下一步的改进方向。（00:47:55）举个例子，Facebook Marketplace就是一个典型案例。Facebook Marketplace团队的创始经理菲奥娜（Fiona）经常提及这一点。Marketplace的设计灵感来源于2016年左右的观察，当时发现Facebook群组中40%的帖子都是关于买卖商品的。（00:48:17）这简直令人惊讶——用户们正在滥用Facebook群组产品进行买卖活动，虽然这并非安全意义上的滥用，而是用户发现了该产品的实用价值。（00:48:29）显然，如果你开发一个更好的买卖产品，用户一定会喜欢它。基于此，Marketplace团队首先推出了专门用于买卖交易的群组，随后又推出了独立的Marketplace产品。（00:48:45）Facebook Dating的诞生也源于类似的观察。研究发现，用户浏览Facebook个人资料时，60%非好友异性用户的浏览行为引发了人们的关注。这表明传统的交友模式存在诸多问题，用户们其实是在互相窥探。基于此，团队决定为这种需求打造专属产品。（00:49:11）潜在需求的概念极具价值。例如，Cowork的诞生也源于类似的发现。过去六个月间，许多用户使用Claude Code并非用于编程：有人用它种西红柿，有人分析基因组，还有人从损坏的硬盘中恢复婚礼照片。（00:49:43）这些完全非技术性的使用案例令人惊叹，开发者们不惜费尽周折通过终端完成任务，这正是产品创新的契机。（00:49:55）早在去年五月，我们就注意到了这一趋势。当时走进办公室时，数据科学家布伦丹（Brendan）的电脑上正运行着Claude Code。他打开了终端界面，我惊讶地问：“布伦丹，你在干什么？” 他成功地掌握了终端操作——这是一款极具工程思维的产品，即便许多工程师都不愿使用终端，因为它是编程的最底层方式。（00:50:26）由此可见，当用户以非预期方式滥用产品来实现自身需求时，就是产品创新最有力的信号。这类产品往往具有特定场景的实用价值。（00:50:50）如今，类似的创新案例不断涌现。
潜在需求的这一有趣的第二维度。这是传统的思维框架——观察人们正在做什么，然后让事情变得更简单，为他们赋能。（00:50:59）：过去六个月我观察到的现代思维框架则略有不同。它是观察模型想要做什么，然后让事情变得更简单。（00:51:10）：所以，当我们最初开始开发Claude Code时，人们设计LLM应用的方式大多是把模型装进一个框子，然后说：“这是我想开发的应用。这是模型要做的事，你只需负责其中的某个组件。以下是如何与这些工具和API交互的指南。”等等。（00:51:28）：但Claude Code反其道而行之。我们说：“产品就是模型。我们要将其暴露出来，围绕它搭建最少的框架，为它提供最基础的工具。这样它就能自行处理事务，决定使用哪些工具，按何种顺序执行任务。”等等。（00:51:41）：我认为这很大程度上源于模型自身的潜在需求。研究领域称之为“顺应分布”——你需要观察模型想要做什么。产品层面而言，潜在需求不过是将这一理念应用于模型而已。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You talked about Cowork. Something that I saw you talk about when you launched that initially is your team built that in 10 days. That's insane.
turns.zh: 你提到了 Cowork。我记得你最初发布它的时候说过，你的团队在 10 天内就开发出来了。这简直太不可思议了。

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It came out, I think it was used by millions of people pretty quickly, something like that being built in 10 days. Anything there? Any stories there other than it was just, "We used a lot of code to build it and that's it"?
turns.zh: 它上线后，我觉得很快就被数百万人使用了，而这东西是在 10 天内开发出来的。还有其他故事吗？除了“我们用了很多代码就开发出来了”之外？

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: Yeah. It's funny. Claude Code, like I said, when we released it it was not immediately a hit. It became a hit over time, and there was a few inflection points. So, one was, like, Opus 4, it just really, really inflected, and then in November it inflected, and it just keeps inflecting. The growth just keeps getting steeper and steeper and steeper every day. (00:52:31): But for the first few months it wasn't a hit. People used it, but a lot of people couldn't figure out how to use it. They didn't know what it was for. The model still wasn't very good. (00:52:40): Cowork when we released it it was just immediately a hit. Much more so than Claude Code was early on. I think a lot of the credit, honestly, just goes to Felix and Sam and Jenny, and the team that built this. It's just an incredibly strong team. (00:52:55): And, again, the place Cowork came from is just this latent demand. Like, we saw people using Claude Code for these non-technical things. And we're trying to figure out, "What do we do?" And so, for a few months the team was exploring, they were trying all sorts of different options. And, in the end, someone was just like, "Okay. What if we just take Claude Code and put it in the desktop app?" And that's, essentially, the thing that worked. (00:53:15): And so, over 10 days they just completely used Claude Code to build it. And Cowork is actually ... There's this very sophisticated security system that's built in. And, essentially, these guardrails to make sure that the model does the right thing, it doesn't go off the rails. (00:53:30): So, for example, we ship an entire virtual machine with it, and Claude Code just wrote all of this code. So, we just had to think about, "All right. How do we make this a little bit safer? A little more self-guided for people that are not engineers." It was fully implemented with Claude Code. It took about 10 days. We launched it early. It was still pretty rough, and it's still pretty rough around the edges. (00:53:50): But this is the way that we learn, both on the product side and on the safety side is we have to release things a little bit earlier than we think, so, that we can get the feedback, so, that we can talk to users. We can understand what people want, and that'll shape where the product goes in the future.
turns.zh: 是啊。这挺有趣的。就像我说的，Claude Code 刚发布的时候并没有立即火爆。它是逐渐火起来的，中间有几个关键节点。比如，Opus 4 那次就火得很突然，之后在 11 月又火了一波，之后火势就越来越猛了。（00:52:31）但最初的几个月它并不火。人们用它，但很多人不知道怎么用，也不知道它是干什么用的。模型当时还不太完善。（00:52:40）而 Cowork 刚发布的时候就火爆了。比 Claude Code 早期火得多得多。我觉得这主要得归功于 Felix、Sam 和 Jenny，还有开发团队。这真是个超强的团队。（00:52:55）而且，Cowork 的诞生源于一个潜在的需求。比如，我们看到人们用 Claude Code 做一些非技术性的应用。我们就想，“我们该怎么做？”于是，团队花了几个月探索，尝试各种方案。最后，有人就说，“好吧。如果我们把 Claude Code 放进桌面应用里呢？” 这招就成功了。（00:53:15）所以，他们用 10 天时间完全用 Claude Code 开发了 Cowork。Cowork 实际上……里面有非常复杂的安全系统。基本上就是一些防护措施，确保模型能正常运行，不偏离轨道。（00:53:30）比如，我们随 Cowork 附赠了一整套虚拟机，而 Claude Code 就自动写了所有代码。所以我们只需要考虑，“好吧，我们怎么让它更安全一点？让非工程师用户更容易上手一点？” 这都是用 Claude Code 实现的。只用了 10 天。我们提前发布了。虽然还有很多粗糙的地方，但这就是我们学习的方式，无论是在产品方面还是安全方面。我们必须比预期更早地发布产品，这样才能获得反馈，跟用户交流，了解他们的需求，这些都会影响产品的未来发展方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I think that point is so interesting, and it's so unique. There's always been this idea, release early, learn from users, get feedback, iterate. The fact that it's hard to even know what the AI is capable of, and how people will try to use it is a unique reason to start releasing things early. So, that'll help you as you exactly describe this idea of what is a latent demand in this thing that we didn't really know? Let's put it out there and see what people do with it.
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得这一点特别有趣，也很独特。一直有这样的理念，早期发布、从用户那里学习、获取反馈、迭代。但要知道人工智能能做什么，以及人们会怎么使用它，这本身就是一个独特的理由，让我们更早地发布产品。所以这对你描述潜在需求很有帮助，特别是我们之前并不知道的那些需求？先把产品推出去，看看人们怎么用。

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: Yeah. And for Anthropic as a safety lab, the other dimension of that is safety, because when you think about model safety there's a bunch of different ways to study it. The lowest level is alignment, and mechanistic interpretability. So, this is when we train the model we want to make sure that it's safe. We, at this point, have pretty sophisticated technology to understand what's happening in the neurons to trace it. (00:54:52): And so, for example, if there's a neuron related to deception, we're starting to get to the point where we can monitor it and understand that it's activating. And so, this is alignment, this is mechanistic interpretability, it's the lowest layer. (00:55:05): The second layer is evals, and this is, essentially, a laboratory setting, the model is in a Petri dish, and you study it. And you put in the synthetic situation and just say, "Okay. Model, what do you do?" And, "Are you doing the right thing? Is it aligned? Is it safe?" (00:55:17): And then the third layer is seeing how the model behaves in the wild. And as the model gets more sophisticated, this becomes so important, because it might look very good on these first two layers, but not great on the third one. (00:55:30): We released Claude Code really early, because we wanted to study safety. And we actually used it within Anthropic for I think four or five months, or something before we released it, because we weren't really sure. Like, this is the first big agent that I think folks had released at that point. It was definitely the first coding agent that became broadly used. (00:55:51): And so, we weren't sure if it was safe. And so, we actually had to study it internally for a long time before we felt good about that. And even since there's a lot that we've learned about alignment. There's a lot that we've learned about safety, that we've been able to put back into the model, back into the product. (00:56:05): And for Cowork, it's pretty similar. The model is in this new setting. It's doing these tasks that are not engineering tasks. It's an agent that's acting on your behalf. It looks good on alignment, it looks good on evals, we tried it internally, it looks good. We tried it with a few customers, it looks good. Now we have to make sure it's safe in the real world. (00:56:21): And so, that's why we release a little early. That's why we call it a research preview. But, yeah. It's constantly improving. And this is really the only way to make sure that over the long-term the model is aligned, and it's doing the right things.

是的。对于Anthropic作为安全实验室而言，另一个维度是安全性，因为当你考虑模型安全性时，有很多不同的研究方法。最底层是对齐（alignment）和机械可解释性（mechanistic interpretability）。所以，在我们训练模型时，要确保其安全性。目前，我们拥有相当先进的技术，可以追踪神经元的活动（00:54:52）。如果有一个与欺骗相关的神经元，我们就能监测到它的激活情况。这就是对齐和机械可解释性，最底层的部分。

第二层是评估（evals），这本质上是一个实验室环境，模型处于受控环境中，然后进行测试。比如，我们会将模型置于合成情境中，观察其行为，评估其是否做出了正确的决策，是否符合道德规范（00:55:05）。第三层是观察模型在真实环境中的表现。随着模型变得越来越复杂，这一点变得尤为重要，因为它在前两层表现出色，但在第三层却可能出现问题。

我们很早就发布了Claude Code，因为我们想研究安全性。实际上，我们在内部使用了四五个月才公开发布，因为当时我们不确定其安全性。这是当时人们发布的首个大型智能体，也是首个得到广泛应用的编码智能体（00:55:51）。我们不确定其安全性，因此内部研究了很久才放心发布。现在，我们对对齐和安全性有了更多认识，并将这些知识反馈到模型和产品中。

对于Cowork，情况类似。模型处于新的环境中，执行非工程类任务。它代表用户行动。在对齐和评估方面表现良好，内部测试效果不错，少数客户反馈也很积极。现在，我们必须确保其在真实环境中安全。

（00:56:05）这就是为什么我们提前发布的原因。这就是为什么我们称之为研究预览。但确实，模型在不断改进。这确实是确保模型长期保持对齐和正确行为的唯一途径。

And the idea is at its core what is your brand? What is it? It's a bunch of neurons that are connected. (00:57:33): And so, what you can do is in a human brain or in an animal brain, you can study it at this mechanistic level to understand what the neurons are doing. It turns out surprisingly a lot of this does translate to models also. So, model neurons are not the same as animal neurons, but they behave similarly in a lot of ways. (00:57:50): And so, we've been able to learn just a ton about the way these neurons work, about this layer or this neuron maps to this concept, how particular concepts are encoded, how the model does planning, how it thinks ahead. A single neuron might correspond to a dozen concepts, and if it's activated together with other neurons this is called super position. And together it represents this more sophisticated concept. (00:58:32): And it's just something we're learning about all the time. turns.zh: 是的。你应该在某个时候邀请克里斯·奥拉（Chris Olah）上播客，因为他是这个领域的专家。他开创了我们称之为"机械可解释性"的研究领域。其核心观点是，你的品牌是什么？它是什么？它就是一群相互连接的神经元（00:57:33）。所以，你可以在人类或动物大脑中，在这种机械层面上进行研究，了解神经元的运作方式。令人惊讶的是，这其中很多研究成果也适用于模型。虽然模型中的神经元与真实神经元不同，但它们在许多方面有着相似的行为（00:57:50）。通过这种方式，我们对神经元的工作机制有了深刻的认识，比如某个层级或某个神经元对应某个概念，特定概念是如何编码的，模型如何进行规划和预测（00:58:03）。很久以前，我们不确定模型只是预测下一个词，还是在做更深层的处理。现在我认为有相当有力的证据表明，它确实在进行更深层的处理。支撑这种处理的结构也相当复杂，随着模型规模的增大，单个神经元对应的概念不再是单一的，一个神经元可能对应十几个概念，如果与其他神经元一起激活，这被称为"超位"。它们共同代表更复杂的概念（00:58:32）。这正是我们一直在探索的内容。对于Anthropic而言，我们认为以安全、对世界有益的方式推动这一领域的发展，正是我们存在的意义，也是Anthropic所有成员的初心（00:58:50）。因此，我们将许多研究成果开源并积极发布，旨在激励其他研究团队以安全的方式开展类似研究。这也是我们为Claude Code所做的，我们内部称之为"向上攀登的竞赛"（00:59:08）。例如，我们为Claude Code推出了开源沙盒，供用户运行智能体，确保其在安全边界内运行，无法访问系统中的所有资源。我们将其开源，使其兼容所有智能体，而不只是Claude Code，因为我们希望让其他团队轻松复现我们的做法（00:59:29）。这一切都遵循"向上攀登的竞赛"原则。我们要确保这一进程顺利推进，而这正是我们手中可以操控的杠杆。

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: I'd probably share a few more things. So, one is don't try to box the model in. I think a lot of people's instinct when they build on the model is they try to make it behave a very particular way. They're like, "This is a component of a bigger system." (01:03:56): I think some examples of this are people layering very strict workflows on a model, for example, to say, like, "You must do step one, and then step two, then step three." And you have this very fancy orchestrator doing this. (01:04:06): But actually almost always you get better results if you just give the model tools, you give it a goal, and you let it figure it out. I think a year ago you actually needed a lot of the scaffolding, but nowadays you don't really need it. (01:04:16): So, I don't know what to call this principle, but it's, like, ask not what the model can do for you. Maybe it's something like this. Just think about how do you give the model the tools to do things. Don't try to over-curate it. Don't try to put it into a box. Don't try to give it a bunch of context upfront. Give it a tool, so, that it can get the context it needs. You're just going to get better results. (01:04:37): I think a second one is maybe actually even a more general version of this principle is just the bitter lesson. And actually for the Claude Code team we have a ... Hopefully, listeners have read this, but [inaudible 01:04:52] this blog post maybe 10 years ago called The Bitter Lesson. And it's actually a really simple idea. His idea was that the more general model will always out-perform the more specific model. And I think for him he was talking about self-driving cars and other domains like this. (01:05:06): But actually there's just so many corollaries to the bitter lesson, and, for me, the biggest one is just always bet on the more general model. And over the long-term. Like, don't try to use tiny models for stuff. Don't try to fine-tune. Don't try to do any of this stuff. There's some applications. There's some reasons to do this, but almost always try to bet on the more general model, if you can, if you have that flexibility. (01:05:29): And so, these workflows are, essentially, a way that ... It's not a general model. It's putting the scaffolding around it. And, in general, what we see is maybe scaffolding can improve performance maybe 10%, 20%, something like this, but often these gains just get wiped out with the next model. So, it's almost better to just wait for the next one. (01:05:50): And I think maybe this is a final principle, and something that Claude Code I think got right in hindsight, from the very beginning, we bet on building for the model six months from now. Not for the model of today. And for the very early versions of the product, it just wrote so little of my code, because I didn't trust it. Because it was, like, Sonnet 3.5. Then it was, like, 3.6, or ... I forget. 3.5 New, whatever name we gave it. (01:06:18): These models just weren't very good at coding yet. They were getting there, but it was still pretty early. (01:06:37): And this is a thing that we first started seeing with Opus 4 and Sonnet 4, and Opus 4 was our first ASL3 class model that we released back in May. And we just saw this inflection, because everyone started to use Claude Code for the first time. And that was when our growth really went exponential. And, like I said, it stayed there. (01:06:56): So, I think this is advice that I actually gave to a lot of folks, especially, people building startups. It's going to be uncomfortable, because your product market fit won't be very good for the first six months. But if you build for the model six months out, when that model comes out, you're just going to hit the ground running, and the product is going to click, and start to work.
turns.zh:
我可能会再分享几点心得。首先，别试图把模型框住。我发现很多人在基于模型进行开发时，总想让它按照特定方式运行。比如，他们会说："这是一个更大系统的一个组件。"（01:03:56）我觉得这类例子很多，比如给模型套上非常严格的工作流，要求用户必须先做步骤一，再做步骤二，最后做步骤三。然后用一个复杂的编排器来实现这些操作。（01:04:06）但实际上只要给模型提供工具、设定目标，让它自己去探索，往往能获得更好的结果。一年前你可能还需要大量脚手架，但现在基本不需要了。（01:04:16）所以，我不知道该怎么给这个原则命名，但可以称之为：别问模型能为你做什么。或许可以这么说：想想如何赋予模型完成任务的工具，而不是过度约束它。别试图把它塞进框架里，别预先给它太多上下文。只需提供工具，让它自己获取所需的信息，这样效果会更好。（01:04:37）第二个原则可能是更通用的，那就是"痛苦的教训"。对于Claude Code团队，我们有一篇……希望听众读过这篇博客，但[01:05:02]可能十年前的博文《痛苦的教训》。其实这个理念很简单。他的观点是，更通用的模型总是胜过更特定的模型。当时他以自动驾驶汽车等领域为例。（01:05:06）但"痛苦的教训"还有很多衍生含义，对我来说，最重要的是永远选择更通用的模型。只要有灵活性，从长远来看就这么做。别用小模型做复杂事务，别微调参数。有些应用场景确实有需求，但多数时候还是要赌一把更通用的模型。（01:05:29）这些工作流本质上是……这不是通用模型，而是围绕它搭建的脚手架。总体来看，我们发现脚手架最多能提升10%、20%的性能，但这些收益往往被后续模型抹平。所以最好等下一个模型。（01:05:50）最后一个原则，或许也是Claude Code事后看来做得对的：从一开始就为六个月后的模型构建，而不是当下的。早期产品版本时，我们的代码量很少，因为不信任模型。当时用的是Sonnet 3.5，后来3.6，或者……记不清了。3.5新版之类的。（01:06:18）这些模型当时编码能力不强，虽然在进步，但还很初级。所以那时模型自动化了一些功能，但大部分代码还是我写的。Claude Code的赌注是，模型最终会足够强大，能自己写大部分代码。（01:06:37）这在Opus 4和Sonnet 4上首次显现，Opus 4是我们五月发布的首个ASL3级模型。当时我们看到用户突然大量使用Claude Code，增长速度陡然提升。
指数级增长。正如我所说，它一直保持着这种增长态势。（01:06:56）：所以，我认为这也是我给过很多人的建议，特别是那些创业公司创始人。前六个月你的产品与市场的契合度不会很高，这会让人很不适应。但如果你提前六个月为这个模式做准备，当这个模式最终推出时，你就能顺势而为，产品也会一举成功，开始发挥作用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And when you say build for the model six months out, what is it that you think people can assume will happen? Is it just generally it will get better at things? Is it just, like, "Okay. It's almost good enough, and that's a sign that it'll probably get better at that thing"? Is there any advice there?
turns.zh: 还有，当你说要在六个月后再构建模型时，你认为人们可以预料到会发生什么？是说它在某个方面会不断进步吗？还是说，比如，“好吧，它已经差不多能做好了，这表明它在这方面可能还会进一步提升”？对此你有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: I think that's a good way to do it. Obviously, within an AI lab, we get to see the specific ways that it gets better.
turns.zh: 我觉得这是一种很好的方法。显然，在人工智能实验室里，我们能亲眼见证它如何不断进步。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: So, it's a little unfair, but also, we try to talk about this. So, one of the ways that it's going to get better is it's going to get better and better at using tools, and using computers. This is a bet that I would make. (01:07:49): Another one is it's going to get better and better for running it for long periods of time. And this is a place ... Like, there's all sorts of studies about this, but if you just trace the trajectory, or maybe even for my own experience when I use Sonnet 3.5 back a year ago, it could run for maybe 15 or 30 seconds before it started going off the rails, and you just really had to hold its hand through any kind of complicated task. (01:08:13): But nowadays with Opus 4.6, on average it'll run maybe 10, 20, 30 minutes unattended, and I'll just start another Claude, and have it do something else. And, like I said, I always have a bunch of Claudes running. And they can also run for hours, or even days at a time. I think there were some examples where they ran for many weeks. (01:08:31): And so, I think over time this is going to become more and more normal where the models are running for a very, very long period of time, and you don't have to sit there and babysit them anymore.
turns.zh: 所以，这有点不公平，但我们也试图谈论这个问题。比如，它会越来越善于使用工具和计算机，这一点我可以打个赌。（01:07:49）另一个方面是，它在长时间运行方面会不断优化。这一点我深有体会。比如，回想一年前我使用 Sonnet 3.5 时的情景，它可能只能运行 15 到 30 秒就会出错，遇到复杂任务时你还得手动操作。（01:08:13）但现在用 Opus 4.6，平均能无需干预地运行 10 到 20 分钟，我可以再启动一个 Claude 去处理其他任务。就像我说的，我通常同时运行多个 Claude。它们甚至能连续运行数小时或数天。我记得有些案例甚至持续了好几周。（01:08:31）所以，我认为随着时间推移，模型能够长时间稳定运行将越来越普遍，人们无需时刻盯着它们了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, you just talked about tips for building AI products. Any tips for someone just using Claude Code, say, for the first time or just someone already using Claude Code that wants to get better. What are a couple pro-tips that you could share?
turns.zh: 你刚刚提到了构建人工智能产品的建议。那么对于刚开始使用 Claude Code 的人，或者已经在用 Claude Code 并希望提升技能的人，有什么实用技巧可以分享吗？

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: I will give a caveat, which is there's no one right way to use Claude Code. So, I can share some tips, but, honestly, this is a dev tool. Developers are all different. Developers have different preferences. They have different environments. So, there's just so many ways to use these tools. There's no one right way. You have to find your own path. (01:09:08): Luckily, you can ask Claude Code. It's able to make recommendations. It can edit your settings. It knows about itself. So, it can help with that. (01:09:17): A few tips that, generally, I find pretty useful. So, number one is just use the most capable model. Currently, that's Opus 4.6. I have maximum effort enabled always. The thing that happens is sometimes people try to use a less expensive model like Sonnet, or something like this, but because it's less intelligent, it actually takes more tokens in the end to do the same task. (01:09:35): And so, it's actually not obvious that it's cheaper if you use a less expensive model. Often, it's actually cheaper and less token-intensive if you use the most capable model, because it can just do the same thing much faster with less correction, less hand holding, and so on. So, that's the first step is just use the best model. (01:09:51): The second one is use plan mode. I start almost all of my tasks in plan mode, maybe, like 80%, and plan mode is actually really simple. All it is is we inject one sentence into the model's prompt to say, "Please don't write any code yet." That's it. There's actually nothing fancy going on. It's just the simplest thing. (01:10:11): And so, for people that are in the terminal it's just shift tab twice. And that gets you into plan mode. For people in the desktop app, there's a little button on the web, there's a little button. It's coming pretty soon to mobile also. And we just launched it for the Slack integration too. So, plan mode is the second one. (01:10:27): And, essentially, the model would just go back and forth with you. Once the plan looks good then you let the model execute. I auto-accept edits after that, because if the plan looks good, it's just going to one shot it. It'll get it right the first time almost every time with Opus 4.6. (01:10:42): And then maybe the third tip is just play around with different interfaces. I think a lot of people when they think about Claude Code, they think about a terminal. And, of course, we support every terminal, we support Mac, Windows, whatever terminal you might use, it works perfectly. (01:10:54): But we actually support a lot of other form factors too. Like, we have iOS and Android apps. We have a desktop app. There's the Slack integration. There's all sorts of things that we support. So, I would just play around with these. And, again, it's, like, every engineer is different. Everyone that's building is different. Just find the thing that feels right to you, and use that. You don't have to use a terminal. It's the same Claude agent running everywhere.
turns.zh: 我要提醒一点，使用Claude Code并没有固定的正确方法。所以，我可以分享一些技巧，但说实话，这只是一个开发工具。开发者各不相同，他们有不同的偏好和环境。因此，使用这些工具的方法千千万万，没有一个标准答案。你必须找到适合自己的路径。（01:09:08）：幸运的是，你可以向Claude Code寻求帮助。它能够提供建议，编辑你的设置，而且它本身对自身有深刻的了解，所以能在这方面提供支持。（01:09:17）：以下是我认为比较实用的几个技巧。首先，使用性能最强的模型。目前，这个模型是Opus 4.6。我一直启用最大努力模式。有些人可能会尝试使用更便宜的模型，比如Sonnet之类的，但由于其智能程度较低，最终完成相同任务反而需要更多代币。（01:09:35）：所以，使用更便宜的模型并不能明显省钱。实际上，使用性能最强的模型往往更便宜且更节省代币，因为它能更快地完成相同任务，同时需要更少的校正和手动干预。因此，第一步就是选择最佳模型。（01:09:51）：第二个技巧是使用计划模式。我几乎所有任务都从计划模式开始，大概80%的情况都是如此。计划模式其实很简单。只需在模型的提示中注入一句话：“请先不要写任何代码。” 就行了。没有什么复杂的操作，就是最简单的设置。（01:10:11）：在终端中，只需按两次Shift+Tab即可进入计划模式。在桌面应用中，网页上有一个小按钮。移动端也很快会推出这个功能。我们刚刚还推出了Slack集成功能。所以，计划模式是第二个技巧。（01:10:27）：然后，模型会和用户反复沟通。一旦计划看起来不错，就让模型执行任务。之后我会自动接受编辑，因为如果计划看起来不错，模型几乎每次都能一次性完成任务。（01:10:42）：第三个技巧是尝试不同的界面。我觉得很多人一想到Claude Code，就会想到终端。当然，我们支持所有终端，包括Mac、Windows等平台，效果都非常好。但我们实际上还支持很多其他设备形式，比如iOS和安卓应用、桌面应用，以及Slack集成等。所以，多尝试一下这些界面吧。再说一次，每个工程师都不一样，每个开发者的情况各异。找到最适合自己的工具，坚持使用就好。不一定非要用终端。Claude代理在所有平台上运行效果都一样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Okay. Just a couple more questions to round things out. What's your take on Codex? How do you feel about that product? How do you feel about where they're going? Just competing in this very competitive space in coding agents.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，再问几个问题来结束这次访谈。你对Codex有什么看法？对这款产品的印象如何？对他们的发展方向有何评价？毕竟在编码代理这个竞争激烈的领域里竞争激烈。

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: Yeah. I actually haven't really used it, but I think I did use it maybe when it came out. It looked a lot like Claude Code to me, so, that was flattering. I think it's actually good to have more competition, because people should get to choose and, hopefully, it forces all of us to do an even better job. (01:11:49): Honestly, for our team, though, we're just focused on solving the problems that users have. And so, for us, we don't spend a lot of time looking at competing products, we don't really try the other products. You want to be aware of them. You want to know they exist. (01:12:03): But, for me, I love talking to users. I love making the product better. I love just acting on feedback. So, it's really just about building a good product.
turns.zh:
是啊。我其实没怎么用过这个产品，但我记得它刚推出的时候我可能用过一下。在我看来，它和Claude Code很像，这挺令人欣慰的。我觉得多些竞争其实是件好事，因为用户应该有更多选择的机会，希望这能促使我们所有人把工作做得更好。（01:11:49）：不过对我们团队来说，我们只专注于解决用户遇到的问题。所以我们不怎么关注竞争产品，也不会去试用其他产品。你需要了解它们的存在，但没必要过分关注。
（01:12:03）：但对我来说，喜欢和用户交流，致力于提升产品质量，及时响应反馈，这才是关键所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe a last question. So, I talked to Ben Mann, co-founder of Anthropic, what to talk to you about. He had a bunch of suggestions, which I've integrated throughout our chat. One question he had for you is what's your plan post-AGI? What do you think you're going to be doing? What's your life like once we hit AGI? Whatever that means.
turns.zh: 最后再问个问题。我和Anthropic的联合创始人本·曼恩聊过，他让我问你一个问题。他提了不少建议，我都融入了我们的聊天内容。他想问你的是：通用人工智能（AGI）时代之后，你有什么计划？你觉得自己会做什么？当我们真正实现AGI时，你的生活会变成什么样？不管AGI最终意味着什么。

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: So, before I joined Anthropic I was actually living in rural Japan. And it was a totally different lifestyle. I was the only engineer in the town. I was the only English speaker in the town. It was just a totally different vibe. A couple times a week I would bike to the farmer's market, and you bike by rice paddies and stuff. It was just a totally different speed. Just complete opposite of San Francisco. (01:12:54): One of the things that I really liked is a way that we got to know our neighbors, and we built friendships is by trading pickles. So, in the town where we lived it was actually, like, everyone made miso, everyone made pickles. And so, I actually got decently good at making miso. And I made a bunch of batches, and this is something that I still make. (01:13:18): Miso is this interesting thing where it teaches you to think on these long time skills that's just very different than engineering, because a batch of white miso takes, at least, three months to make. And a red miso is, like, two, three, four years. You just have to be very patient.
turns.zh:
在加入Anthropic之前，我实际上住在日本乡下。那是一种完全不同的生活方式。我是镇上唯一的工程师，也是唯一会说英语的人。氛围截然不同。每周有几次，我会骑自行车去农贸市场，路过稻田之类的地方。节奏完全不同，和旧金山完全相反。（01:12:54）：我特别喜欢的一点是，通过制作泡菜，我们认识了邻居，建立了友谊。在我们住的那个镇上，每个人都会做味噌，每个人都会做泡菜。所以我现在做味噌还是挺拿手的。我做过好几批，现在还在继续做。
（01:13:18）：味噌这种东西很有趣，它教会你思考那些需要长期积累的技能，这和工程学完全不同。比如一批白味噌至少需要三个月才能完成，而红味噌则需要两到四年。你必须非常有耐心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: You mix it up, and then you just let it sit. You have to be very, very patient. So, the thing that I love about it is just thinking in these long time skills. And, yeah. I think post-AGI or if I wasn't at Anthropic, I'd probably be making miso.
turns.zh: 你把材料混合起来，然后静置等待。要有极大的耐心。所以我喜欢味噌的地方，就是能让我用长远的视角去思考问题。是啊。我觉得在AGI时代之后，或者如果我不在Anthropic工作，我可能会去制作味噌。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this answer. Ben asked me to ask you about what's the deal with you and Miso. And so, I love that you answered it. Okay. So, the future might be just going deep into miso, getting really good at making miso. Amazing. Boris, this was incredible. I feel like we're brothers now from Ukraine. (01:14:08): Before we get to our very exciting lightning round, is there anything else that you wanted to share? Is there anything you wanted to leave listeners with? Anything you want to double down on?
turns.zh: 我喜欢你的这个回答。本让我问你关于你和味噌的关系。我很高兴你能回答这个问题。好的，未来或许你可以深入研究味噌，真正成为制作味噌的高手。太棒了。鲍里斯，这次交流太棒了。我感觉我们现在就像来自乌克兰的兄弟了。（01:14:08）：在我们开始激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么想分享的吗？有什么想留给听众的吗？有什么值得深思的地方吗？

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: Yeah. I think I would just underscore for Anthropic since the beginning, this idea of starting at coding, then getting to tool use, then getting to computer use has just been the way that we think about things. And this is the way that we know the models are going to develop, or the way that we want to build our models. And it's also the way that we get to learn about safety, study it, and improve it the most. (01:14:40): So, everything that's happening right now around just Claude Code becoming this huge multi-billion dollar business, and now all of my friends use Claude Code, and they just text me about it all the time. So, this thing getting big. (01:14:55): In some ways, it's a total surprise, because this isn't the ... We didn't know that it would be this product. We didn't know that it would start in a terminal, or anything like this. (01:15:04): But, in some ways, it's just totally unsurprising, because this has been our belief as a company for a long time. At the same time, it just feels still very early. Like, most of the world still does not use Claude Code, most of the world still does not use AI. So, it just feels like this is 1% on, and there's so much more to go.
turns.zh:
是啊。我觉得从一开始我就想强调，人类中心主义的理念——从编码入手，再到工具使用，再到计算机应用——一直是我们思考问题的方式。这也是我们认为模型会发展的方式，也是我们想要构建模型的方式。同时，通过这种方式，我们能最有效地学习安全知识、研究安全问题并不断改进。

（01:14:40）：所以，目前Claude Code发展得如此之大，已经成为价值数十亿美元的巨头，而我身边所有朋友都在用它，还老是给我发消息聊这事。这种火爆程度真是令人惊讶。

（01:14:55）：但从某种角度看，这一点也不意外，因为这正是我们公司长期秉持的信念。与此同时，感觉这一切才刚刚起步。毕竟全球大部分人还没用过Claude Code，大多数人甚至都不了解AI技术。所以目前只算1%的发展阶段，后面还有更广阔的空间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, man. That's insane to think, seeing the numbers that are coming out. You guys just raised a bazillion dollars. I think Claude Code alone is making $2 billion revenue. Anthropic, I think the number you guys put out, you're making $15 billion in revenue. It's insane to just think this is how early it still is, and just the numbers we're seeing.
turns.zh: 天哪。看到这些数据真是不可思议。你们刚募集了巨额资金。我觉得Claude Code单独就创造了20亿美元营收。Anthropic，你们公布的数据是150亿美元营收。想想现在才起步阶段，再看看这些数字，真是令人震惊。

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. It's crazy. And the way that Claude Code has kept growing is, honestly, just the users. Like, so many people use it. They're so passionate about it. They fall in love with the product, and then they tell us about stuff that doesn't work, stuff that they want. (01:15:55): And so, the only reason that it keeps improving is because everyone is using it, everyone is talking about it, everyone keeps giving feedback. And this is just the single most important thing. And, for me, this is the way that I love to spend my days just talking to users, and making it better for them.
turns.zh: 是啊是啊是啊。这太疯狂了。Claude Code能持续发展，最关键的还是用户。太多人使用它，对它充满热情，爱上这个产品，然后反馈问题和需求。正因为大家都在用、都在讨论、不断反馈，产品才能不断优化。这才是最重要的。对我来说，每天和用户交流、优化产品，就是最充实的生活。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And making miso.
turns.zh: 还有做味噌。

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: And making miso. Well, the miso is not super evolved. You've just got to wait.
turns.zh: 还是做味噌。嗯，味噌还没完全做好。你就耐心等着吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You've just got to wait. Well, Boris, with that, we've reached our very exciting lighting round. I've got five questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 耐心等着吧。好的，鲍里斯，接下来是激动人心的提问环节。我有五个问题要问你，准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: Let's do it.
turns.zh: 开始吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First question, what are two or three books that you find yourself recommending most to other people?
turns.zh: 第一个问题，哪两三本书是你最常向别人推荐的？

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: I'm a big reader. I would start with a technical book. It is Functional Programming in Scala. This is the single best technical book I have ever read. It's very weird, because you're probably not going to use Scala. And I don't know how much this matters in the future now, but there's this just elegance to functional programming and thinking in types, and this is just the way that I code, and the way that I can't stop thinking about coding.
turns.zh: 我是个书迷。我会从技术书籍入手。《Scala中的函数式编程》。这是我读过的最棒的技术书籍。说来奇怪，你可能根本用不到Scala。不过现在看来这也不重要了，但函数式编程和类型思维的优雅之处确实令人惊叹。这就是我编程的方式，也是我对编程的痴迷所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: So, you could think of it as a historical artifact. You could think of it as-
turns.zh: 所以你可以把它视为历史遗物。你可以把它看作——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A deep cut.
turns.zh: 一部冷门佳作。

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: ... something that will level you up.
turns.zh: ……能让你更上一层楼的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this. A never before mentioned book. My favorite.
turns.zh: 我太爱这本书了。一本从未被提及的书。我的最爱。

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: Oh, amazing. Amazing. Okay. Second one is Accelerando by Stross. My big genre is sci-fi. Probably sci-fi and fiction. Accelerando is just this incredible book. And it's just so fast-paced. The pace gets faster and faster and faster. And I just feel like it captures the essence of this moment that we're in more than any other book that I've read, just the speed of it. (01:17:23): And it starts as a lift-off is starting to happening, and is starting to approach the singularity. And it ends with this collective lobster consciousness orbiting Jupiter. And this happens over the span of a few decades or something. So, the pace is just incredible. I really love it. (01:17:41): Maybe I'll do one more book. The Wandering Earth. Wandering Earth by Liu Cixin. So, he's the guy that did Three Body Problem. I think a lot of people know him for that. Actually I think Three Body Problem was awesome, but I actually liked his short stories even more. So, Wandering Earth is one of the short story collections, and he just has some really, really amazing stories. (01:18:01): And it's also just quite interesting to see Chinese sci-fi, because it has a very different perspective than western sci-fi, and the way that, at least, he, as a writer, thinks about it. So, it's just really, really interesting to read, and just beautifully written.
turns.zh: 哦，太棒了。太棒了。好的。第二本是斯特罗斯的《加速》。我的主攻领域是科幻，可能科幻和小说都有。《加速》就是一本令人惊叹的书。节奏快得惊人，越往后越快。我觉得它比我读过的任何书都更能捕捉到我们所处时代的精髓——那种快节奏感。（01:17:23）故事从即将升空的场景开始，逐渐逼近奇点，最后以集体意识的龙虾在木星轨道上运行收尾。这整个过程只发生在几十年间。所以节奏感简直绝了。我太爱它了。（01:17:41）或许我再推荐一本书。刘慈欣的《流浪地球》。对，他就是写《三体》的那个人。我想很多人都是因为《三体》认识他的。其实我觉得《三体》很棒，但我更爱他的短篇小说。《流浪地球》是短篇小说集之一，里面的很多故事都非常精彩。（01:18:01）读中国科幻也很有趣，因为它和西方科幻有着截然不同的视角，至少就刘慈欣作为作家的思考方式而言是这样。所以读起来非常有趣，文笔也极其出色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's so interesting how sci-fi has prepared us to think about where things are going. It creates these [inaudible 01:18:21] models of like, "Okay. I see. I've read about this sort of world."
turns.zh: 科幻如何让我们为事物的发展方向做好准备，这真是太有趣了。它创造了这些[01:18:21]模型，比如，“好吧，我懂了。我读过这样的世界。”

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: Yeah. I think, for me, this was the reason that I joined Anthropic actually, because, like I said, I was living in this rural place. I was thinking these long-time skills, because everything is just so slow out there. At least, compared to SF. And just all the things that you do are based around the seasons, and it's based around this food that takes many, many months. That's the way that social events were organized. That's the way that you organize your time. (01:18:48): You go to the farmer's market, and it's persimmon season, and you know that, because there's 20 persimmon vendors. And then the next week the season is done, and it's, like, grape season. And you see this. So, it's these long-time skills. (01:19:00): And I was also reading a bunch of sci-fi at the time. And just being in this moment, I was just thinking about these long-time skills. I know how this thing can go. And I felt like I had to contribute to it going a little bit better. (01:19:12): And that's actually why I ended up at Ant. And Ben Mann was also a big part of that too.
turns.zh:
是啊。我觉得这就是我加入Anthropic的原因，因为就像我说的，我当时生活在乡下。那里的一切节奏都太慢了。至少和科幻比起来，慢得多。你做的所有事情都围绕着季节转，围绕着需要数月才能成熟的食物。社交活动也是根据季节安排的。时间规划也是如此。（01:18:48）你去农贸市场，正值柿子季，你能分辨出来，因为有20个柿子摊贩。下周季末，又到了葡萄季。你能亲眼见证这些周期。就是这些长周期技能。（01:19:00）当时我也在读很多科幻书籍。身处那个当下，我就在思考这些长周期技能。我知道事态可能会如何发展，我觉得自己有责任让它朝着更好的方向发展。
（01:19:12）这就是我最终加入Ant的原因。本·曼恩在其中也起了很大作用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like I want to do a whole podcast just talking about your time in Japan, and the journey of Boris through Japan to Anthropic. But we'll keep it short. I'll quickly recommend a sci-fi book to you if you haven't read it. Have you read Fire Upon The Deep?
turns.zh: 我觉得我应该做一期完整的播客，专门聊聊你在日本的经历，以及鲍里斯从日本到Anthropic的旅程。但我们还是长话短说。如果你还没读过，我会快速给你推荐一本科幻书。《深火》你读过吗？

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: This is Vinge. Right? Yeah.
turns.zh: 这是文奇的作品，对吧？对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: It's great.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. That one, it's so interesting from an AI/AGI perspective. So few people have read that. So, [inaudible 01:19:41]. Yeah. It's like [inaudible 01:19:42]-
turns.zh: 好的。从人工智能/通用人工智能的角度来看，那本书非常有趣。读过它的人太少了。所以，[听不清 01:19:41] 。是的。就像 [听不清 01:19:42] 一样——

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: I really like the ... Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. I like Deepness in the Sky also. I think [inaudible 01:19:49] sequel. Right?
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢……嗯。嗯。嗯。我也喜欢《天空深处》。我觉得[听不清 01:19:49] 是续集，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. I think so.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊，是啊。我觉得是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. It's very long, and complex to get into, but so good. Okay. We'll keep going through our lightning round. Do you have a favorite recent movie or TV show you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 是啊。这部剧很长，很复杂，但真的很棒。好吧。我们继续进行快速问答环节。你最近有没有特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: So, I actually don't really watch TV or movies. I just don't really have time these days. I did watch ... I'm going to bring up another Liu Cixin, but the Three Body Problem series on Netflix I really loved. I thought that was a great rendition of the book series.
turns.zh: 其实我最近不太看电视或电影，因为实在没时间。不过我确实看过……我要再提一下刘慈欣的《三体》系列，我在Netflix上看的，真的很棒。我觉得这部剧对原著的改编非常出色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, the common pattern across AI leaders is no time to watch TV or movies, which I completely understand. Is there a favorite product you've recently discovered that you really love?
turns.zh: 所以，AI领域的领导者普遍都很忙，没时间看电视或电影，这我完全理解。你最近有没有发现什么特别喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: I'm going to shill a little bit, and just say Cowork, because this is, legitimately, the one product that's been pretty life-changing for me just because I have it running all the time. And the Chrome integration, in particular, is just really excellent. So, it's been like ... It paid a traffic fine for me, it canceled a couple subscriptions for me. Just the amount of tedious work it gets out of the way is awesome. (01:20:45): I also don't know if it's a product, but maybe also another podcast that I really love ... Obviously, besides Lenny is-
turns.zh: 我要稍微推荐一下Cowork，因为这款产品真的改变了我的生活。它能全天候运行，特别是与Chrome的集成功能，非常棒。比如，它帮我交过交通罚款，取消过几项订阅服务……它能处理很多繁琐的工作，真是太棒了。（01:20:45）：我也不知道这算不算产品，或许还有个我特别喜欢的播客……除了Lenny之外——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Obviously.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: Yeah. It's the Acquired podcast by Ben and David. It's just super awesome. I feel like the way that they get into business history, and bring it alive is really, really good. And I would start with the Nintendo episode if you haven't listened to it.
turns.zh: 是啊，Ben和David主持的Acquired播客，真的超棒。我觉得他们解析商业历史的方式特别生动，如果你还没听过《任天堂》那期节目，强烈推荐。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great tip. With Cowork, just so people understand if they haven't tried this, basically, you type something you want to get done and it can launch Chrome, and just do things for you. I saw someone went on pat leave from Anthropic, and you had to fill out these medical forms for him, these really annoying PDFs where it just loads up the browser, logs in, fills them out, [inaudible 01:21:29].
turns.zh: 好建议。关于Cowork，方便大家理解的话，如果没用过的话，它基本上就是你输入待办事项，它就能启动Chrome，帮你完成任务。我看到有人休产假，Anthropic需要填写医疗表格，特别烦人的PDF文件，打开浏览器，登录，填写表格，[01:21:29无法听清]。

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: Yeah. Exactly. Exactly. And it actually just works. Like, we tried this experiment a year ago, and it didn't really work, because the model wasn't ready, but now it actually just works and it's amazing. (01:21:39): I think a lot of people just don't really understand what this is, because they haven't used an agent before, and it just feels very, very similar, to me, to Claude Code a year ago. But, like I said, it's just growing much faster than Claude Code did in the early days. So, I think it's starting to break through a bit.
turns.zh: 是啊，完全正确。现在真的能用了。比如，一年前我们做过这个实验，但模型没准备好，不过现在真的能用了，太棒了。（01:21:39）：我觉得很多人不了解这个产品，因为他们没用过智能助手，对我来说，它和一年前的Claude Code很像。但就像我说的，它发展的速度比Claude Code早期快多了。所以，我觉得它正在逐渐突破。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And there's also this Chrome extension that you mentioned that you could just leave standalone that sits in Chrome, and you could just talk to Claude looking at your screen, at your browser, and have it do stuff, have it tell you about what you're looking at, summarize what you're looking at, things like that.
turns.zh: 还有你提到的那个Chrome扩展程序，你可以让它独立运行在Chrome里，你只要看着屏幕，看着浏览器，就能和Claude对话，让它帮你做事，比如告诉你正在看的内容，汇总你正在看的内容之类的。

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: Exactly. Exactly. For people that are just learning to use Cowork, the thing I recommend is, so, you download the Claude desktop app, you go to the Cowork tab, it's right next to the code tab. The thing that I recommend doing is start by having it use a tool. So, clean up your desktop, or summarize your email, or something like this, or respond to the top three emails. It actually just responds to emails for me now too. (01:22:29): The second thing is connect tools. So, if you say, "Look at my top emails," and then sends back messages ... Or put them in a spreadsheet, or something. But, for example, I use it for all my product management. So, we have a single spreadsheet for the whole team. There's a row for engineer. Every week, everyone fills out a status. And every Monday, Cowork just goes through and it messages every engineer on Slack that hasn't filled out their status. And so, I don't have to do this anywhere.
turns.zh: 没错。没错。对于刚开始学习使用Cowork的人，我建议这样做：首先下载Claude桌面应用，进入Cowork标签页，它就在代码标签页旁边。我推荐先让它使用某个工具。比如，清理桌面、汇总邮件、回复前三封邮件之类的。现在它甚至能自动回复我的邮件了。（01:22:29）第二步是连接工具。例如，当你说“看看我的重要邮件”，它会反馈信息……或者把这些信息导入电子表格之类的。但我个人把它用于所有产品管理工作。我们整个团队共用一个电子表格，每周工程师们会填写状态报告。每周一，Cowork会自动给所有未填写状态报告的工程师发送提醒消息，这样我就不用手动处理了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: And this is just one prompt. It'll do everything. And then the third thing is just run a bunch of Claudes in parallel. So, in Cowork you can have as many tasks running as you want. So, it's, like, start one task, I have this project management thing running, then I'll have it do something else, then something else, and then I'll kick these off. And then I just go get a coffee while it runs.
turns.zh: 这只是一个示例提示。它能处理所有任务。第三步是并行运行多个Claude实例。在Cowork中，你可以同时运行多个任务。比如，先启动一个项目管理任务，再做其他事，最后启动这些任务。我只需去泡杯咖啡，让它自动运行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a post I'll link to that shares a bunch of ways people use what was previously Claude Code, and now just you can do through Cowork. Because a lot of this is just like, "Wow. I hadn't thought I could use it for that." And once you see ... These examples I think are what people need to hear of just like, "Oh, wow. I didn't know I could do that." [inaudible 01:23:26].
turns.zh: 我会分享一个帖子，里面有很多以前用Claude Code的人现在如何通过Cowork实现这些功能。因为很多功能让人惊叹：“哇，我没想到还能这样用。”一旦看到这些例子，人们就会意识到“哦，原来还能这样做。”[01:23:26不可听清]

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: I think a lot of this was also some of this was also inspired by you, Lenny. You had this post about ... It was, like, 50 non-technical use cases for Claude Code, or something like this. So, actually one of our PMs used that as a way to evaluate Cowork before we released it, and I think at the point where Cowork was able to do, like, 48 out of the 50, they were like, "Okay. It's pretty good."
turns.zh: 很多功能的灵感还来自你，Lenny。你之前写过一篇关于Claude Code的50个非技术用例的帖子，对吧？实际上，我们的一位产品经理在发布Cowork前用这个帖子评估了它，结果发现Cowork能实现50个用例中的48个，他们就觉得：“好吧，它还不错。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I did not know that. That is awesome. I've become an eval.
turns.zh: 哇。我都不知道这个。太棒了。我现在成了一个评测员。

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: Yeah. [inaudible 01:23:54].

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. I feel like I'm valuable to the future of AI.
turns.zh: 太神了。我感觉自己对AI的未来很有价值。

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: This is, like, reverse breaking through.
turns.zh: 这简直是反向突破。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. That is so cool. Wow. Okay. I wonder what those last two are. Anyway, okay. Two more questions. Do you have a favorite life motto that you often come back to in work or in life?
turns.zh: 哇。这太酷了。好的。我想知道最后两个是什么。不管怎样，再问两个问题。你有没有一个在工作或生活中经常回想的座右铭？

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: Use common sense. I think a lot of the failures that I see, especially, in a work environment is people just failing to use common sense. Like, they follow a process without thinking about it. They just do a thing without thinking about it, or they're working on a product that's not a good product or not a good idea, and they're just following the momentum, and not thinking about it. (01:24:32): I think the best results that I see are people thinking from first principles, and just developing their own common sense. If something smells weird then it's probably not a good idea. So, I think this is the single advice that I give to coworkers more than anything too.
turns.zh: 用常识思考。我认为我见过的很多失败案例，尤其是在职场环境中，都是因为人们没有运用常识。比如，他们盲目遵循流程，却不加思考；做事前不深思熟虑，或者他们正在开发的产品既不实用也不明智，却随波浮沉，毫不深思。（01:24:32）：我认为我见过的最佳成果，是人们从第一性原理出发，逐步培养自己的常识。若某件事闻起来不对劲，那很可能就不是个好主意。所以，这是我最常给同事的建议。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I feel like that alone could be its own podcast conversation. What is common sense? How do you build? But we'll keep this short. Final question. So, you've got more active on Twitter/X. I'm curious just why and just what's your experience been with Twitter? The world of Twitter. Because you get a lot of engagement on Twitter/X.
turns.zh: 我觉得单就这个话题就能做一期播客讨论。什么是常识？如何培养？但我们先长话短说。最后一个问题，你在Twitter/X上越来越活跃了。我很好奇原因何在？你在Twitter的体验如何？毕竟你在这上面收获了大量互动。

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: So, for a long time I used Threads exclusively, because I actually helped build Threads a little bit back in the day. And I also just like the design. It's a very clean product.
turns.zh: 很久以来我一直只用Threads，因为我早期参与过Threads的开发，而且我很喜欢它的设计。这是个非常简洁的产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: I just really like that. I started using Threads, because actually I was bored. So, in December, I was in Europe-
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢它。我开始用Threads是因为当时无聊。12月我在欧洲旅行——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Started using Twitter you mean.
turns.zh: 你是说开始用Twitter吧。

turns.speaker: Boris Cherny
turns.en: Oh, yeah. Yeah. Yeah. I started using Twitter, because I was bored. So, my wife and I, we were traveling around in Europe for December. We were just nomad-ing around. We went to Copenhagen, we went to a few different countries. And, for me, it was just a coding vacation. So, every day I was coding, and that's my favorite kind of vacation, just code all day. It's the best. (01:25:43): And, at some point, I just got bored, and I ran out of ideas for a few hours. I was like, "Okay. What do I want to do next?" And so, I opened Twitter, I saw some people tweeting about Claude Code, and then I just started responding. And then I was like, "Okay. Maybe actually a thing I should do is just look for bugs that people have. Maybe people have bugs," or feedback they have. And so, introduce myself, asked for it, people had a bunch of blogs and feedback. (01:26:07): And I think they were surprised by the pace at which we were able to address feedback nowadays. For me, it's just so normal. Like, if someone has a bug, I can probably fix it within a few minutes, because I just started Claude, and as long as the description is good, it'll just go and do it, and then I'll go do something else, and answer the next thing.
